slides.title: Nibras answers Al-Nuha University's students from 2,977 pages
slides.text: The case study for four days Nibras answers Al-Nuha University's students from 2,977 pages Regulations in Arabic and English, amended by circulars over five years Course pages and study plans with tables, some of them scanned Service guides and news, written for students A warehouse of enrolments for statistical questions Some pages are Restricted: staff only Your role Kawthar Al-Beladi, the retrieval engineer. The model is not your job; what it reads is. The decision owner Dr. Lubna Al-Harithi, vice-rector for digital transformation, wants numbers before the pilot widens.

slides.title: A good answer can hide bad retrieval, and the reverse
slides.text: Why measure retrieval on its own A good answer can hide bad retrieval, and the reverse Question "How many absences before I am denied the final exam?" → Retrieval the top 5 pages the model will read → Generation the answer written from those pages Judging only answers A model can answer from memory with the page missing, or paraphrase a superseded rule fluently. Judging retrieval Was the page that answers it in the top 10, and how high? Cheap, repeatable, no model needed.

slides.title: Relevance has degrees: grade it 0 to 3
slides.text: Relevance in grades Relevance has degrees: grade it 0 to 3 Grade Meaning Judged for "deadline to withdraw from a course" 3 The page that answers it Article 25: Withdrawal from a course 2 Answers part of it, or needs another page Circular 2026-031, which amends Article 25 1 On topic, does not answer Article 26: Postponement of study 0 Not relevant, or never judged Article 58: Transfer from another university Write the guideline first. Two judges who read the same guideline disagree less, and the test set outlives the people who made it.

slides.title: Judge a pool, not the whole corpus
slides.text: Which pages get judged Judge a pool, not the whole corpus 1 · Run several systems BM25, dense, anything you have ↓ 2 · Take each one's top results merge, remove duplicates ↓ 3 · Judge the pool unjudged pages count as not relevant 396 judged pairs for 60 queries in test set v1 The bias. A new system that finds pages no pooled system found is scored as wrong on them. Add its top results to the pool before you compare.

slides.title: Recall, reciprocal rank and nDCG measure different failures
slides.text: Three numbers, three questions Recall, reciprocal rank and nDCG measure different failures Recall at 10 Of the relevant pages, how many are in the top 10? The model cannot read what is not there. Reciprocal rank 1 over the rank of the first relevant page. Does the answer come first? nDCG at 10 Rewards grade 3 above grade 1 and high ranks above low ones, scaled 0 to 1. dcg = sum((2**grade[p] - 1) / log2(rank + 1) for rank, p in enumerate(top10, 1)) ndcg = dcg / ideal_dcg # the same sum over the best possible order

slides.title: An inverted index maps each word to the pages that contain it
slides.text: Lexical search An inverted index maps each word to the pages that contain it Term Pages withdraw Article 25, Circular 2026-031, guide/withdrawal postpone Article 26, guide/postponement semester 924 of the 2,617 Public pages A query looks up its words, not every page: fast at any size Exact words only: "withdrawal" and "withdraw" are different keys unless you stem Every database has one: SQLite FTS5, PostgreSQL full-text search, OpenSearch

slides.title: BM25 rewards rare words and saturates repeated ones
slides.text: How BM25 weighs words BM25 rewards rare words and saturates repeated ones Rarity "postpone" in 9 pages weighs far more than "semester" in 924. Saturation The tenth "postpone" in a page adds little over the third. Length A match in a short page counts more than in a long one. CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE idx USING fts5(id UNINDEXED, text); SELECT id, bm25(idx) FROM idx WHERE idx MATCH '"withdraw" OR "course" OR "deadline"' ORDER BY bm25(idx) LIMIT 10; -- lower is better in FTS5

slides.title: One Arabic word has several spellings, and BM25 sees each as a stranger
slides.text: What Arabic does to word matching One Arabic word has several spellings, and BM25 sees each as a stranger Variation Written Also written Hamza on alif الأولى الاولى Final ya and alif maqsura المستوى المستوي Ta marbuta and ha الجامعة الجامعه Diacritics and tatweel الدِّراسة الدراسة Clitics والطلاب الطلاب What goes wrong. Students type fast on phones and skip the hamza; the regulation is typeset carefully. Raw matching punishes exactly the users you serve.

slides.title: Normalise and lightly stem both the pages and the query
slides.text: The fix Normalise and lightly stem both the pages and the query 1 · Normalise remove diacritics and tatweel; unify alif, ya, ta marbuta → 2 · Light stem strip ال, و, ب and common suffixes → 3 · Index the analysed words, not the raw text The classic bug Normalising the pages but not the query, or the reverse: every match fails silently. Light, not deep A root-based stemmer merges words with different meanings. Light stemming removes affixes only.

slides.title: Normalisation lifts Arabic recall from 0.34 to 0.44 and dialect from 0.05 to 0.25
slides.text: Measured in Lab 1.2 Normalisation lifts Arabic recall from 0.34 to 0.44 and dialect from 0.05 to 0.25 Arabic, raw 0.340 Arabic, normalised 0.435 English, either 0.432 Dialect, raw 0.05 Dialect, normalised 0.25 Recall at 10 on test set v1. nDCG@10 overall: 0.473 raw, 0.538 normalised. Query p95 latency 6.7 ms on a laptop.

slides.title: Dialect fails on vocabulary, which no spelling rule repairs
slides.text: Read the failures, not only the score Dialect fails on vocabulary, which no spelling rule repairs Studentابي اوقف دراستي ترم كم مره يسمحون Top resultArticle 36, lateness to an exam Takeaway. اوقف دراستي means "postpone my study", but the regulation says تأجيل الدراسة. No spelling rule bridges that; other words can: the corpus's own, or a model of meaning.

slides.title: A word the index never saw matches nothing, however it is spelled
slides.text: Read the index's vocabulary A word the index never saw matches nothing, however it is spelled A student asks: ماده ما كملتها وش يكتبون بالسجل ("a course I did not finish, what goes on my record?") Query word, analysed Public pages that hold it ماد 119 سجل 43 ما 7 كملت · يكتب · وش 0 What BM25 returns Circular 2024-090 first. Article 43, on the incomplete grade, is not in the top 10. How to read it The words that carry the question have a count of 0: the student and the regulation use different words.

slides.title: Rewrite into the corpus's own words, and keep only rewrites the index holds
slides.text: Query rewriting Rewrite into the corpus's own words, and keep only rewrites the index holds Words added to the query Pages per added word Article 43 ناقص 0 not in top 10 معلق 0 not in top 10 تقدير غير مكتمل 16 · 10 · 1 first Take the target from the corpus : a title or a heading, run through the same analyser Check it : every added word occurs in the index, or the rewrite does nothing Add, do not replace : keep the student's words Measure it on the dialect slice and on the rest What goes wrong. A rewrite that sounds right but uses words the corpus never uses fails silently: the ranking does not move.

slides.text: Checkpoint Why did Arabic recall not move? Kawthar adds a normaliser to the indexing pipeline and rebuilds the index. Arabic recall at 10 stays at 0.34. English is unchanged too. BM25 cannot rank Arabic text The Arabic queries are all in dialect Normalisation needs a deep root stemmer to work The queries are not passed through the same normaliser

slides.title: An embedding places texts with similar meaning close together
slides.text: Dense retrieval An embedding places texts with similar meaning close together A model turns each page into 384 numbers; the query too Search is a dot product of the query with every page Multilingual models put an Arabic question near an English answer No word has to match: "drop a course" can find "withdrawal" The two models of Lab 1.3 multilingual-e5-small and paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2: open weights, 384 dimensions, small enough for a laptop processor or a free Colab runtime.

slides.title: e5 expects "query:" and "passage:" in front of its inputs
slides.text: Read the model card e5 expects "query:" and "passage:" in front of its inputs model.encode("query: " + question) model.encode("passage: " + page_text) nDCG@10, dense e5 with prefixes without Arabic 0.375 0.354 English 0.639 0.615 All 0.507 0.484 What goes wrong. Nothing fails loudly. Skip one line of the model card and you lose a few points everywhere, without an error message.

slides.title: Embedding the corpus takes minutes; each query adds tens of milliseconds
slides.text: What embedding costs Embedding the corpus takes minutes; each query adds tens of milliseconds 7.3 min to embed all 2,977 pages with e5, laptop processor 82 ms e5 query embedding, 95th percentile 252 ms MiniLM query embedding, 95th percentile Measured once when the supplied vectors were made: 300 pages in 44.1 s (e5) and 27.4 s (MiniLM), on a shared laptop. Your Colab numbers will differ; the ratio between indexing and querying will not.

slides.title: Half-way through a model change, search sees only the pages already re-embedded
slides.text: Changing the embedding model Half-way through a model change, search sees only the pages already re-embedded MiniLM index, pages moved to e5 nDCG@10 top 10 from moved pages 25% 0.138 100% 50% 0.288 100% 75% 0.399 100% 100% 0.507 100% 0.70 to 0.89 cosine of one e5 query with e5 pages −0.15 to 0.09 the same query with MiniLM pages What goes wrong. Both models give 384 numbers, so a mixed index raises no error. The old pages simply never compete.

slides.title: A new model means a new index: re-embed everything, then switch queries and pages together
slides.text: The procedure A new model means a new index: re-embed everything, then switch queries and pages together 1 · Build beside embed the whole corpus with the new model into a second index → 2 · Measure the test set by language on the new index → 3 · Switch together query model and index in one step; keep the old one to roll back Record the model Store the model's name with the index and refuse a query vector from any other. Plan the time The full re-embedding is the cost of the change: 7.3 minutes here, much longer at a million pages.

slides.title: Exact search compares with every page; HNSW walks a graph of neighbours
slides.text: Indexes for vectors Exact search compares with every page; HNSW walks a graph of neighbours Exact (flat) every page, every query: perfect recall, linear time ↓ HNSW a layered graph, coarse to fine: a few hundred comparisons 2,617 Public pages e5 MiniLM Overlap with exact top 10 0.922 0.995 HNSW index size 4.73 MB 4.73 MB Flat index size 4.02 MB 4.02 MB HNSW p95 0.53 ms 0.52 ms Exact p95 1.15 ms 1.29 ms

slides.title: Hybrid search and reranking
slides.text: Session 4 Hybrid search and reranking Fuse two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion Rerank candidates with a cross-encoder Decide on a reranker from its gain and its 95th-percentile latency 04

slides.title: Lexical and dense search fail on different queries
slides.text: Hybrid search Lexical and dense search fail on different queries BM25 finds Course codes, circular numbers, article numbers, exact names: "CSC 301", "2025-118". Dense finds Paraphrases, everyday words, the other language: "drop a course", a question in English about an Arabic page. The idea. Run both, then merge the two rankings into one. The question is how to merge two lists whose scores are on different scales.

slides.title: BM25 scores run from 0.3 to 28; cosine scores from 0.78 to 0.93
slides.text: Why you cannot add the scores BM25 scores run from 0.3 to 28; cosine scores from 0.78 to 0.93 BM25 range 0.3 to 28.4 Cosine range 0.78 to 0.93 Weighted score fusion nDCG@10 alpha 0.3 0.570 alpha 0.5 0.566 alpha 0.7 0.556 What goes wrong. Add raw scores and BM25 decides everything. Normalise them and you add a weight to tune, and it moves with every corpus change.

slides.title: Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 / (60 + rank) from each list
slides.text: Use ranks, not scores Reciprocal rank fusion adds 1 / (60 + rank) from each list def rrf(rankings, k=60): score = defaultdict(float) for ranking in rankings: for rank, page in enumerate(ranking, 1): score[page] += 1 / (k + rank) return sorted(score, key=score.get, reverse=True) Test set v1 recall@10 MRR nDCG@10 BM25 normalised 0.433 0.729 0.538 dense e5 0.401 0.691 0.507 RRF of the two 0.455 0.776 0.570

slides.title: A cross-encoder reads the query and each candidate together
slides.text: The second stage A cross-encoder reads the query and each candidate together 1 · First stage BM25 and dense, fused: top 30 in milliseconds → 2 · Rerank a model scores each (query, page) pair: 30 model calls → 3 · Top 5 what the generator reads Why it is better It sees both texts at once, so it can judge whether the page answers this question. Why it is slow One forward pass per candidate, every query. Nothing can be computed ahead.

slides.title: Retrieval can only find what the parser wrote down
slides.text: Corpus preparation Retrieval can only find what the parser wrote down PDF or scan what the university publishes → Parser text and tables, or nothing → Chunks what gets indexed → Search Day 1's methods What goes wrong. A parsing failure looks like a retrieval failure: the page "is never found". Score the parser on its own, against reference text, before you tune search.

slides.title: A text-layer parser reads what the PDF stores; a layout-aware one reads the page
slides.text: Two families of parser A text-layer parser reads what the PDF stores; a layout-aware one reads the page Parser A · text layer Fast and cheap. Reads the characters the PDF holds, in the order it holds them. A scan holds no characters; Arabic may come out in presentation forms and reversed order. Parser B · layout-aware Slower. Recognises text from the image and finds table structure. Makes its own errors: similar letters confused. Examples of the families: pypdf and pdfminer for text layers; Docling, Unstructured, Tesseract and open-weight document vision models for layout and recognition.

slides.title: A small parsing model or a general vision model: score both on your pages
slides.text: Inside the layout-aware family A small parsing model or a general vision model: score both on your pages Small specialised parsing model Trained only to read documents: layout, reading order, table structure, characters. Runs on modest hardware and costs little per page. Weak on layouts it never saw. General vision model Reads the page image and follows an instruction, such as "return this table as Markdown". Flexible on odd layouts. Costs more per page and can write fluent text that is not on the page. What goes wrong. A misread letter looks like a mistake. An invented word looks like text. Only a score against reference pages, by page type, shows which one you have.

slides.title: Word error rate: the edits that turn the output into the reference, per word
slides.text: Score the text Word error rate: the edits that turn the output into the reference, per word def words(text): text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text) return re.findall(r"\w+", U.normalise(text)) def wer(ref, out): r, o = words(ref), words(out) return edit_distance(r, o) / len(r) Normalise first, or you score typography, not content Two swapped words cost two edits: a toy of three words scores 0.667 An empty output scores 1.0, every word missing

slides.title: A table is right only when each cell is in its row and column
slides.text: Score the tables A table is right only when each cell is in its row and column Compare the parsed table with the reference cell by cell: same row, same column, same text Text can be perfect and the table worthless: "3" and "IND 212" on one line do not say which course they belong to Study plans are mostly tables: a question like "how many credit hours is CSC 301" lives in one cell Takeaway. Report text and table scores separately. A parser can win one and lose the other.

slides.text: The common default Fixed windows cut tables wherever the word count falls window 1 ... | Total | 14 | | ### Year 1 · Semester 2 | Code | Course | Credit hours | Prerequisite | |---|---|---|---| | ACC 101 | Introduction to Financial ... window 2 ... Accounting | 3 | UNI 105 | | ACC 112 | ... What goes wrong. The window that holds "ACC 101" may not hold "Semester 2", and neither names the programme. slides.title: Answerable at 3: does a top-3 chunk hold everything the answer needs?
slides.text: Score chunking by the questions it answers Answerable at 3: does a top-3 chunk hold everything the answer needs? Each of the 20 table questions lists the strings the answer needs: "Semester 6" and "MTH 301" A question is answerable when one of the top 3 chunks contains all of them No model needed, so the score is cheap and repeatable Why not recall? Chunkings make different units, so there are no shared relevance judgements. Answerability compares them on the same questions.

slides.title: A recommendation names the evidence and when to revisit it
slides.text: The recommendation, written down A recommendation names the evidence and when to revisit it Recommendation. Chunk study plans by semester heading with the plan title and year carried into each chunk, and never cut inside a table. Revisit if plans gain long prose sections, where windows of a fixed size may retrieve better. Evidence : answerable at 3, 0.65 against 0.25, on 20 questions Scope : study plans; regulations and news may chunk differently Revisit : a condition you can check, not "later"

slides.title: The issue date says when a rule was written; the effective date says when it counts
slides.text: Read both dates The issue date says when a rule was written; the effective date says when it counts question What is the maximum study load in a regular semester? (asked on 1 November 2026) Article between 12 and 20 credit hours Circular 2026-140 issued 2026-10-05, effective 2027-01-01: between 12 and 18 answer 12 to 20 today; 18 from 1 January 2027 What goes wrong. "Newest first" picks the circular, which is not yet in force.

slides.title: Give every version a validity interval and filter by today's date
slides.text: The fix Give every version a validity interval and filter by today's date Article 17 version valid from valid to Regulation text start 2025 amendment Circular 2025-118 its effective date open Parse the circular for the article it amends and its effective date Close the previous version's interval when the next takes effect At query time keep chunks valid on the question's date In the lab: 93 chunks, 33 of them amendments; 63 are valid on 1 November 2026.

slides.title: Near-duplicate copies crowd the top results with the same text
slides.text: Duplicates Near-duplicate copies crowd the top results with the same text Circulars are forwarded, re-posted by colleges, and copied into news Compare chunks as sets of word shingles (runs of 3 words) and their Jaccard overlap Copies measured 0.62 to 0.71 overlap; a threshold of 0.5 catches them 8 near-duplicate copies dropped in Lab 2.3 Keep the original. Drop the copy, keep the official circular's metadata: its dates are the ones that count.

slides.title: A staleness test asks a question and fails if the old answer comes first
slides.text: Make it a test A staleness test asks a question and fails if the old answer comes first for t in CHANGED: # 15 questions, Arabic and English top = search(valid_on(TODAY), [t["q"], t["q_ar"]])[0] assert t["expect"] in top.text, t["qid"] assert t["stale"] not in top.text, t["qid"] 3 → 15 of 15 tests passing, before and after Run it on every rebuild A new circular, a re-parse or a new model can break it again.

slides.title: A tool description tells the model when to call it, not only what it does
slides.text: The description is the interface A tool description tells the model when to call it, not only what it does def keyword_search(query: str, k: int = 5) -> list[dict]: """Keyword search (BM25, Arabic normalised). Best for exact words: course codes such as "CSC 301", circular numbers such as "2025-118", article numbers and names. English or Arabic.""" The function's docstring becomes the tool's description in the schema the model sees Examples of when to use it beat a list of features The stretch writes a misleading description and watches the choices change

slides.title: Call the model, run the tool it asks for, append the result, repeat
slides.text: The loop, in twelve lines Call the model, run the tool it asks for, append the result, repeat messages = [system, {"role": "user", "content": question}] for step in range(max_steps): reply = chat(messages, tools=schemas) if not reply.tool_calls: return reply.content # the answer for call in reply.tool_calls: result = TOOLS[call.name](**call.args) result = json.dumps(result)[:budget_chars] # the context budget messages.append(tool_message(call.id, result)) return "step budget spent"

slides.title: Offload: write the result to a file and return a stub
slides.text: The fix Offload: write the result to a file and return a stub def offload(result, limit=1500): if count_tokens(result) <= limit: return result path = OUT / f"list_courses_{n}.txt" path.write_text(result) return json.dumps({"file": path.name, "lines": n_lines, "pages": n_pages, "preview": result[:200], "hint": "search it with grep_file"}) Nothing is lost The full result is one tool call away. A tool for the file grep_file(file, pattern) returns the matching lines and their count.

slides.text: How to score SQL Execution accuracy: run the query and compare the result with the reference Not the text Two different queries can both be right. Not "it ran" A query that runs can return a wrong number. The result Equal to the reference answer, within rounding for rates. Benchmarks such as BIRD report execution accuracy for the same reason.

slides.text: Session 4 Diagnosing failures by component Attribute a failure to parsing, retrieval, ranking or generation Fix the weakest component and measure again Explain why failures move down the ladder 04

slides.title: "The model is bad" is not a diagnosis
slides.text: Diagnosing failures "The model is bad" is not a diagnosis Students reported 20 wrong answers from Nibras Each has a trace: the parsed text, the 50 candidates, the top 5 the model read, the answer The question for each: which component lost the answer first? Why it matters A new model does not fix an empty parse. A new parser does not fix a prompt. Fix the component that failed, then measure again.

slides.title: Walk down the pipeline and stop at the first component that lost the answer
slides.text: The attribution ladder Walk down the pipeline and stop at the first component that lost the answer 1 · Parsing are the needed words in the parsed text? → 2 · Retrieval is the page among the 50 candidates? → 3 · Ranking is it in the top 5 the model read? → 4 · Generation does the answer contain the needed words? Order matters. A page that was never parsed cannot be retrieved; blaming retrieval would send you to the wrong fix.

slides.text: Measured in Lab 4.4 Parsing lost the most answers: 7 of 20 parsing 7 retrieval 5 ranking 5 generation 3 Attribution of the 20 reported failures; it matches the component each failure was built to fail in.

Six fixed failures now reach the model with the right page; their recorded answers are still wrong because no model was re-run. One now fails at retrieval.
